message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
You've got this. A small, simple room is a good first floor. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it, so there's a little ridge where they meet. You can feel it with your bare feet or catch a toe on it, and it shows up when light hits the floor at a low angle.

It's a particular risk with long tiles like your 30 × 60 cm ones, because they're often very slightly bowed. If you lay them in a brick pattern, avoid the classic half-tile offset. Shifting each row by a third of a tile instead (about 20 cm) keeps the high middles away from the low ends. Tile levelling clips, a cheap spacer-and-wedge system, also help keep edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour for pale grey tiles

Go for a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. Avoid white or very pale grout on a floor; it's what makes floors look dirty within weeks. A mid-grey hides everyday grime but still looks neat with pale grey porcelain.

Look for a grout labelled stain-resistant or mould-resistant. If it's a standard cement grout, seal it once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** Tiling the whole floor and sitting the toilet on top gives a cleaner finish. It saves fiddly cuts around the base of the pan, and if you ever replace the toilet, the floor underneath is already complete. Just plan your cut around the soil pipe.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so you need **24 tiles** to cover the floor exactly.
- Add 10%: 26.4, which rounds up to **27 tiles**.
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **buy 4 boxes** (32 tiles).

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with nothing spare, so don't be tempted.

Four boxes leaves about 5 spare tiles beyond the 10%, which is useful. Big tiles are easy to break while cutting, and a couple of leftovers are handy for repairs later. Check that all the boxes come from the same batch, since shades can vary slightly between batches.

Your room is exactly 4 tiles by 6 tiles on paper, but don't count on that. Grout joints add width, walls are rarely perfectly square, and you'll need to cut around the toilet pipe.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names],
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting floor tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from the tile cutter, roughly [9 am to midday]. We'll keep it to that window as best we can.
>
> Thank you as well for being so patient with the skip on the drive for the last couple of weeks. It's much appreciated, and it should be gone soon.
>
> [Your names]

## Three tips for your first floor

1. **Preparation is most of the job.** The floor underneath must be solid, clean and flat; check it with a long straight edge. Long tiles are unforgiving of dips and humps, and most lippage comes from what's underneath. If it's a wooden floor, ask about overboarding with plywood or tile backer board first.

2. **Dry-lay before you mix anything.** Lay the tiles out loose to plan where the cuts land. Aim for even cuts at both edges, and avoid thin slivers at the doorway where they'd be most visible. Start at the far side of the room and work back toward the door, so you don't tile yourself into a corner.

3. **Get full adhesive coverage.** For large tiles, use a notched trowel of the size the adhesive bag recommends for your tile (usually around 10–12 mm). Also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile ("back-buttering"). Mix small batches so the adhesive doesn't start to set. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the back is fully covered. Hollow spots under tiles lead to cracks later.

The videos do make it look easier than it is, mostly because they cut out the slow parts. Take your time, keep a damp sponge handy, and don't worry if the first row takes ages. It gets quicker.
